Selling a house in Phoenix, AZ

Phoenix is the biggest city in Arizona and the county seat, which means a single sale touches city hall, the Maricopa County recorder and the county treasurer. An estimated 1,665,481 people lived here in July 2025, across roughly 518 square miles.

Homeowners occupy 57.3 percent of homes, a lower share than you would see in smaller Valley cities, and a typical owner-occupied house was valued at $420,700 over 2020 to 2024. Median gross rent was $1,582. A tenant living in your house limits showings and may slow a buyer's closing.

Urban villages and rezoning

Phoenix has 15 urban villages, running from Ahwatukee Foothills to South Mountain, and each one has a Village Planning Committee named by the mayor and council. The committees hear rezoning cases, general plan amendments and text amendments, then send a recommendation to the Planning Commission and the City Council.

If your buyer hopes to change what the lot is used for, the village committee hears the case first. That adds time the buyer has to plan for, so a buyer with big plans may want a longer inspection period or a different property. A buyer who only wants to live in the house will never see this step, and neither will you.

Heat and inspections

Air conditioning and roofing get the most scrutiny from inspectors here. A typical year brings about 111 days with highs of at least 100 degrees, and the record is 122 degrees. The urban heat island keeps nights warm too, with the normal low at or above 80 degrees for an average of 74 days each summer.

Gather before you list:

  • Service dates and invoices for each cooling unit
  • The roof's age and any repairs
  • Records of shade, insulation or window work done to cut cooling costs

Which school district is your address in?

Your address could be in any of 33 school districts, a leftover from annexations that absorbed older districts into the city. Twenty-one elementary districts, four high school districts and four unified districts cover the city, and well over 100 charter schools operate in it.

Phoenix Union High School District enrolls more than 27,000 students at 16 schools. Glendale Union, Tempe Union and Tolleson Union cover just parts of the city, and among the unified districts only Paradise Valley blankets Phoenix. Boundaries are tangled enough that a call to the district office is the only safe way to name a school for an address.

Short-term rental permits

After Arizona Senate Bill 1168, Phoenix moved from registration to a permit for any short-term rental. Staff must grant or refuse a complete application within 7 days. The terms:

  • A $250 fee, for the first permit and for each renewal, with applications through the SHAPE PHX portal.
  • A state Transaction Privilege Tax license, plus a rental status update at the Maricopa County Assessor.
  • A Notice of Intent, sent by certified mail, to adjoining neighbors and to any registered HOA or neighborhood association within 600 feet.
  • Violations decided in court carry minimum penalties of $500, $1,000 and $3,500, and three in a year can suspend a permit for 12 months.
  • For a property with an accessory dwelling unit that received a certificate of occupancy on or after September 14, 2024, the owner must file a notarized attestation that the owner lives on the property.

Questions about one permit go to the city's short-term rental staff: vacation.rental@phoenix.gov or 602-534-9723.

Recording the deed

The Maricopa County Recorder, at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, files Phoenix deeds. Doors are open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and no appointment is needed to file in person. Each deed travels with an Affidavit of Property Value or an exemption code, and recording runs $30.00 a document. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, buyer and seller attest to the price, parcel number and sale date. Title companies usually do the filing for the seller.

The treasurer's office or your title company can say if the first half on your parcel has been paid. Title will also divide the year's bill between buyer and seller.

Selling a house with a permit or a tenant

Rental history changes the conversation with a buyer. A house that has held a short-term rental permit comes with a neighbor notice, a state tax license and possible penalties on record. Gather those papers and the permit number, and ask the city's staff about its status before the first showing. A buyer who wants to keep renting needs the full picture, and one who plans to live there still wants to know nothing is pending.

A house with a long-term tenant is a different case. Showings depend on the tenant's cooperation, and a buyer who needs to move in will ask when possession is possible. Talk to the tenant early, put any agreed move-out date in writing, and tell your title company so the closing timeline accounts for it.

If an accessory dwelling unit sits on the lot, check its certificate of occupancy date. That date decides whether the owner-occupancy attestation applies to a short-term rental permit.

Getting around Phoenix

Streets follow a flat grid, and freeways link the villages. Sky Harbor International Airport flies nonstop to more than 100 cities, and Valley Metro runs a 38.5 mile light rail system with an A Line and a B Line. If your house is near a rail stop or an on-ramp, say so in the listing.

From accepted offer to closing

Listing or cash, a Phoenix sale runs in this order.

  1. Gather the cooling, roof, rental permit and tax papers.
  2. Confirm the school district for the address with the district office.
  3. Accept an offer and open escrow.
  4. Escrow staff request loan payoffs, allocate the year's tax and draft the deed and affidavit.
  5. On closing day the deed goes to the Maricopa County Recorder.
  6. Once the deed is recorded and payoffs clear, your proceeds are released.

Selling for cash removes loan approval, often the longest wait. It does not remove recording, the tax split or rental permit questions. If tax is owed on the house, tell escrow early so the payoff can come out of your proceeds. It also helps to keep your own copy of the permit, the deed and the settlement statement for later questions from a lender or a city office.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a permit to rent my Phoenix house short term?

Yes. A city permit is required, at $250 for the first one and for each renewal. You also need a state Transaction Privilege Tax license and must mail neighbors a certified notice.

How many urban villages does Phoenix have?

Fifteen. A Village Planning Committee in each one hears rezoning cases before the Planning Commission does.

Which county office records a Phoenix deed?

The Maricopa County Recorder, downtown at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200. Expect the $30.00 fee and an affidavit or exemption code.

When are Phoenix property taxes due?

One half is due October 1 and the other March 1. Late status begins after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 for the first and after 5:00 p.m. on May 1 for the second.

How many school districts serve Phoenix?

Thirty-three. That mix includes elementary, high school and unified districts, so confirm any specific address with the district office.

Your options for a fast Tucson sale

Start by choosing a listing with an agent, a for-sale-by-owner effort or an as-is cash purchase. Whichever you pick, the closing in Pima County ends the same way: escrow at a title company, a deed recorded by the Pima County Recorder and a sales affidavit attached to the deed.

A regular listing works for a well-kept house when you can wait on a buyer's mortgage. Cash makes more sense if repairs were put off, a tenant lives there, probate is pending or a tax bill needs clearing fast. Whatever the route, plan for the inspection: buyers here test the roof, the cooling system and the drainage. Tucson covers a large desert basin, and a house can have little in common with one a few miles away.

Pull together these papers first:

  • Payoff letters from lenders, plus the Assessor parcel number
  • Permit paperwork for casitas, room additions, pool work or replaced HVAC and water heaters
  • Utility status, since a house with power or gas off for months needs a reconnect permit
  • Your current Pima County Treasurer tax statement

Tucson home values

Tucson has 548,371 residents, up from 542,629 at the 2020 census. Owners live in 51.8% of homes. Median home value is $266,200, median rent is $1,145, and the median household earns $57,073 across 228,020 households.

Those are citywide figures. A midtown house near the University of Arizona and a foothills property can sit far apart on price, so compare recent sales on your own street.

After monsoon rain, buyers' inspectors look at roof flashing, stucco cracks, window seals and drainage around the foundation. The monsoon season officially starts June 15, and storms can last into September. The Santa Cruz River is dry much of the year but floods in heavy seasonal rain, so ask the city whether your parcel falls in a floodplain or wash zone before you set a price. Paving and grading in washes, hillside zones and floodplains always needs a permit.

Permits that come up in a Tucson sale

Most residential work in Tucson needs a permit and inspection. The Planning and Development Services Department (PDSD) runs the process through the Tucson Development Center Online portal. PDSD is in the Public Works Building at 201 N. Stone Avenue, and the phone is 520-791-5550.

The owner is responsible for plans and a permit for:

  • New or replacement water heaters, furnaces, heat pumps and air conditioners, with load and sizing calculations for HVAC
  • Electrical service increases and panel replacement or repair
  • Detached accessory structures over 200 square feet, such as storage sheds
  • Porches, additions, garages and remodels of existing structures
  • Walls and fences, which need a zoning site plan review, and a building permit with engineered design above 7 feet

Review time depends on the project. The Express Lane handles same-day items such as residential electrical and plumbing work. Fences and pools go to the Fast Lane with a 15-day target, and alterations and new buildings go to the Standard Lane with a 30-day goal. Interior finishes such as paint, carpet and cabinets need no permit, and neither does a like-for-like toilet swap.

Unpermitted work and vacant houses

You can still get a permit for finished work, though the same requirements apply. Submit a full set of construction drawings and complete the inspections. The owner should stop any ongoing work until the permit exists.

A vacant house raises a second issue. A permit is required to reconnect electric or gas service if the utility has been off to a residential structure for 6 consecutive months. The permit costs $135.59 and covers an inspection for obvious code or life-safety problems. Property in a Historic Preservation Zone, Neighborhood Preservation Zone or designated Historic Landmark needs a permit for any development, plus a design review.

Casitas are allowed, one per residential lot, if they meet size and height standards. Rental units count as commercial property for permit purposes. Homeowners may use the owner-builder exemption under A.R.S. 32-1121 for their own residence, but it does not apply to any project that requires a building permit or where materials and labor exceed $1,000. Permit approval does not override HOA covenants on the property.

If a permit turns out to be missing, tell the buyer early. Many cash buyers will take the house as it stands and adjust their price, which can be faster than finishing inspections yourself, but get that agreement in writing and keep any drawings or receipts you have for the work.

Pima County property tax due dates

Tucson house taxes go to the Pima County Treasurer, who sends the bill. Anything over $100 splits into two payments.

InstallmentDue dateDelinquent after 5 p.m.
First halfOctober 1November 1
Second halfMarch 1May 1

The tax year 2026 second-half postmark deadline is May 3, 2027. Interest on the first installment is waived if you pay the whole year before 5 p.m. on December 31. Call the Treasurer at 520-724-8341.

Have the title company order a payoff so any unpaid tax is taken from your proceeds when you close. If you want to contest your value, petition the Pima County Assessor within 60 days of the postmark on a Notice of Value mailed on or before March 1. Disputes concern value, and the tax itself stays payable while you wait.

Recording the deed

Documents that transfer real property go to the Pima County Recorder with a complete legal description and an Affidavit of Property Value under A.R.S. 11-1133. A deed submitted without a complete affidavit is rejected and returned.

An exempt transfer must be accompanied by the Arizona Department of Revenue exemption letter and number. Formatting rules apply too: an original signature, print of at least ten point, a page no bigger than 8.5 by 14 inches and a 2-inch top margin on page one. Photo identification is required from anyone who brings documents in person. Staff cannot offer legal advice, so lean on your title company or attorney.

In a typical sale, the title company orders payoffs and searches the record, you and the buyer sign, funds are released, and the deed goes to the Recorder. Take a photo ID to the signing table, along with your lender payoff letter and any lease if tenants live there.

Frequently asked questions

How long can a sale take in Tucson?

The route and the state of the title decide it. Once title work is clear, a cash buyer can close when you say, but a buyer with a mortgage adds appraisal and loan time. Ask your title company what it needs for a Pima County payoff and recording.

Do I need a permit to replace my water heater or air conditioner in Tucson?

Yes. Tucson requires a permit and inspection for new or replacement water heaters, furnaces, heat pumps and air conditioners. HVAC permits need load and sizing calculations.

Can I sell a Tucson house that has unpermitted work?

You can sell it, but disclose the work and ideally permit it first. Tucson allows permits for work already done if you supply full drawings and pass inspections. Ask PDSD at 520-791-5550 what applies to your address.

Who collects property tax on a Tucson house?

Collection belongs to the Pima County Treasurer, while the Pima County Assessor sets values. November 1 and May 1 are the dates after which each half is late.

What is required to record a deed in Pima County?

The deed needs a full legal description and an Affidavit of Property Value. An exempt transfer instead carries the Department of Revenue exemption letter and number, and anyone filing in person shows photo identification.

Selling a house in Mesa, AZ

Mesa homeowners can sell three ways: hire an agent, go it alone, or take a cash offer. Whichever you pick, the sale finishes with a deed filed at the Maricopa County Recorder and a tax bill divided between you and the buyer. With an estimated 513,656 people in July 2025, Mesa is a big market, and details like which street you are on, which school district applies and how old the roof is can move the price and the timeline.

For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home was valued at $408,000, and 64.4 percent of homes were lived in by their owners. About one household in three rents, so your likely buyer may be an investor who intends to keep the house as a rental.

Which part of Mesa is your house in?

Mesa measures about 18 miles from Price Road on the west to Meridian Road on the east. Center Street is the dividing line between West Mesa and East Mesa in the street numbering, so a buyer reading your address already knows the half.

Before you quote any city rule, find the parcel on the city's Explore Mesa map. Some parcels carry a Mesa postal address yet sit on a Maricopa County island outside the city, where Mesa licenses and permits have no force.

School boundaries do not follow the city line either:

  • Mesa Public Schools covers nearly all of the city.
  • Gilbert Public Schools, Higley Unified and Queen Creek Unified take in the southern edge.
  • A thin strip on the west falls to the Tempe Elementary School District and Tempe Union High School District.

Ask the district for its boundary map before you tell any buyer which school the house feeds.

Freeways, heat and inspection prep

Commute access is an easy selling point. U.S. 60, known as the Superstition Freeway, crosses town. Loop 101 skirts the west side and Loop 202 passes the north and east. Light rail runs about four miles along Main Street, from Sycamore to Gilbert Road, and Mesa Gateway Airport lies in the southeast.

Summers are harsh. East Mesa averages a July high of 105.9 degrees, which is why inspectors spend time on air conditioning and roofing. Have these ready before the first showing:

  • Service records for the cooling system
  • The roof's age and repair history
  • Permit papers for any patio, addition or pool

Seller-supplied records answer the inspector's first questions and keep a repair request from becoming a price cut.

Short-term rental license

A house that guests have rented for 29 days or less at a time needs a Mesa short-term rental license, and the city grants it to the owner only. Conditions:

  • Renewal paperwork and the $250 fee per rental unit are due at the Licensing office at least 45 days before expiration.
  • The unit must hold a current Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax license showing its location.
  • Neighbors beside and around the unit get a notice with the Mesa license number, the address and an emergency contact.

Call Licensing before you sell and ask what becomes of the license once ownership changes. Whatever they tell you belongs in the conversation with your buyer.

Recording the deed

The Maricopa County Recorder takes the deed together with an Affidavit of Property Value, or an exemption code marked on the document. A.R.S. 11-1133 has buyer and seller (or their agents) certify the price, the parcel number, the date, the financing and whether an owner will live there or tenants will. Without a full affidavit or an exemption notation, the recorder turns the deed away.

Recording costs $30 per document in the usual case, with a few listed exceptions. You can file at 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200 in Phoenix, Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Recorder staff will not choose an exemption code for you. Most sellers never visit, because the title or escrow company builds and submits the package.

The next payment on the calendar is March 1. Your title company can say whether the first half is already paid on your parcel and how the current year's bill will be shared at closing.

If a half is unpaid when you sell, tell the title company early. Escrow can settle what is owed out of your proceeds, but only if the amount is known before the closing date. Bring the most recent bill to your first meeting with them, and ask for the tax split in writing so you can compare it with the settlement statement.

Before you accept an offer

Most Mesa delays trace back to paperwork nobody went looking for until escrow opened. Work through this list first.

  1. Pull up the parcel on the Explore Mesa map and confirm it lies in the city.
  2. Request the school boundary map from the right district.
  3. Collect your cooling, roof and permit records.
  4. If the house was a rental, phone Licensing about the license.
  5. Locate your latest tax bill and check what has been paid.
  6. Tell the title company how you are selling so it can start the deed and affidavit.

Selling for cash can spare you the showings, the repair haggling after an inspection and the weeks spent waiting on a buyer's loan. The deed filing and the tax split still happen at closing, so keep those on your list.

One last habit pays off: write down who you spoke to at each office and what they said. If a Licensing clerk tells you the rental license ends at transfer, you will want that on record when the buyer asks.

What happens at closing

On closing day the escrow officer collects the signed deed, confirms payoffs on any loans or liens, divides the year's property tax and sends the deed and affidavit to the recorder. After the filing, the buyer is the owner of record and your proceeds are released.

If something looks wrong on the settlement statement, such as a tax split that seems off or a payoff you did not expect, ask the escrow officer before you sign. Changing a figure is simple before the deed is recorded and a good deal harder afterward.

Keep copies of the signed deed, the settlement statement and any rental license correspondence. A later buyer, a lender or the county may ask for them, and they are easy to lose in a move.

Frequently asked questions

Does a house sale in Mesa need an Affidavit of Property Value?

Yes, unless the deed carries an exemption code. The affidavit travels with the deed or sale contract, and the recorder will not accept a deed lacking a complete one or an exemption notation.

What does Maricopa County charge to record a deed?

The usual fee is $30 per document. A few exceptions exist, so look at the recorder's fee page for your specific document, or ask your escrow company.

Is every address with a Mesa mailing address inside Mesa city limits?

No. A parcel on a Maricopa County island can have a Mesa postal address and still lie outside the city's jurisdiction. Check the Explore Mesa map or call Licensing before relying on a city rule.

When does the second half of the property tax come due?

March 1. It becomes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. The first half is due October 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1.

Which school district serves a house in Mesa?

Mesa Public Schools serves almost all of the city. Gilbert Public Schools, Higley Unified or Queen Creek Unified serve the south, and the Tempe districts cover a small western portion. Confirm your address with the district.

Ways to sell a Gilbert house

Gilbert sellers have three doors to choose from: an agent, a do-it-yourself sale, or a buyer who pays cash and wants the house exactly as you leave it. Each door swaps time, effort and money in its own mix. Condition, deadline and tolerance for prep work should decide it.

Gilbert at a glance

Gilbert is a town in Maricopa County, southeast of Phoenix, south of Mesa, northeast of Chandler and northwest of Queen Creek. Gilbert Public Schools covers most addresses, though sections fall under Chandler Unified, Mesa Public Schools or Higley Unified. Look the district up by street address before you advertise it.

Permits and town rules before listing

For permit questions, reach the Town's Development Services office at (480) 503-6700 or onestopshop@gilbertaz.gov. Customer hours are extended for most services, from 7 a.m. until 6 p.m. Monday to Thursday, while building, engineering and fire inspections keep separate schedules.

Did you finish a patio, pool, garage conversion or accessory dwelling without pulling a permit? Ask Development Services what record exists before you commit to a contract. The permit page lists a residential fee calculator, an accessory dwelling unit guide, pool fence rules, a noise ordinance and a permit extension request form, and each one speaks to something an inspector is likely to ask. An HOA's covenants may restrict exterior changes, so pull those papers early.

Short-term and long-term rentals

Nightly rentals in Gilbert need a Town license, approved by the Council in June 2023. The license and renewal fee is $250 as of October 1, 2026. Under A.R.S. 9-500.39 the state keeps a town from banning them, but a permit, emergency contact details and liability coverage can be required. Send licensing questions to ShortTermRentals@gilbertaz.gov.

If tenants live there, A.R.S. 33-1902 requires you to maintain a registration with the county assessor and refresh it within ten days of a change. Review it before listing.

Deed recording and the affidavit of value

The deed goes to the Maricopa County Recorder with an affidavit of value attached. Without it the deed comes back, unless an exemption is written on its face (A.R.S. 11-1133). Buyer and seller sign it side by side. The form covers parcel number, sale date, price and financing, and adds two questions: is personal property 5% or more of the price, and will the buyer live there or rent?

Under A.R.S. 11-1134, these transfers can skip the affidavit if the deed cites the exemption:

  • Gifts
  • Court-ordered conveyances
  • Nominal-consideration transfers inside the family circle (spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, siblings)
  • Corrective deeds repeating one already recorded

Filing costs $30 an instrument (A.R.S. 11-475), and that number swallows the $2 transfer fee in A.R.S. 11-1132. The office at 602-506-3535 answers general questions but will not coach you through forms. For the documents themselves, rely on a title company or attorney. Property tax and valuation appeals

Two payments make up a Gilbert tax year, both billed by Maricopa County. A.R.S. 42-18052 fixes the late dates.

A weekend November 1 pushes the first-half date, as the county calendar shows. The escrow officer splits the year's tax between you and the buyer at closing. Ask how, and make sure no half is left owing.

Challenging the Assessor's number is possible, though the calendar is tight. Between January 1 and March 1 the Notice of Value arrives. Sixty days from its mailing date is your window for the petition for review, and the Assessor replies by August 15. A refusal leaves 25 days to appeal to the State Board of Equalization. A lawsuit must be filed by December 15 of the notice year or within 60 days of the last administrative ruling.

Know the limit before you spend effort. Only full cash value can be contested, and your bill rests on the limited property value, which generally cannot grow faster than 5% a year.

What Gilbert buyers tend to ask

Buyers in a town this size arrive with a short list. Which school district is the address in? How far is the freeway on-ramp, and what does the drive to Phoenix look like at rush hour? Is there an HOA, and will its rules block a pool fence or a casita? Can guests stay by the night, or does the owner need a Town license first?

You win time by answering before you are asked. Print the district name, note the nearest Loop 202 interchange, attach the HOA covenants and state plainly if the house has been rented out. A listing sheet that answers these questions reads as an organized seller, and an organized seller gets fewer low offers built on fear of the unknown. The same sheet helps a cash buyer move faster, since fewer surprises means a quicker yes.

Price talk is the other half of it. With values this high, a buyer's agent will lean on any visible repair to argue for a discount, so a fresh coat of paint on weathered trim or a serviced air conditioner can pay for itself. If you would rather not do repair work at all, that is a legitimate reason to look at an as-is sale, where the buyer carries the work and you carry nothing but the paperwork.

Before you ask for offers

Assemble a sale folder holding the parcel number, newest tax bill, HOA contact, repair list and permit records. Whoever opens it should be able to price the house quickly. If the house is vacant, inherited or tenant-occupied, say so up front, since closing mechanics change.

Want speed? Ask for a written offer stating the closing date and your take-home amount, then compare it with a listing price once repairs, agent fees, carrying costs and slow weeks are deducted. Read the whole agreement before signing, ideally after a title company or attorney has.

The title company retires your mortgage and any liens at the table, records the deed with the county and pays you the remainder. Bring photo identification. Ask ahead of time whether keys, garage openers and HOA fobs should change hands that day.

Do I need an affidavit of value to sell a house in Gilbert?

Yes, unless the transfer is exempt. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires buyer and seller to sign an affidavit that goes with the deed, and the Maricopa County Recorder refuses a deed without it unless an exemption such as a gift or a court-ordered conveyance is noted on the deed.

When are Gilbert property taxes due?

Half is due October 1 and half is due March 1. The first half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, except that bills of $100 or less are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31.

Does Gilbert allow short-term rentals?

Yes, with a Town license. Arizona law prevents a town from prohibiting short-term rentals, and Gilbert requires a license under its June 2023 ordinance. The license and renewal fee is $250 as of October 1, 2026, and ShortTermRentals@gilbertaz.gov handles questions.

How long do I have to appeal my Gilbert home's value?

You have 60 days from the date the Maricopa County Assessor mailed the Notice of Value. The petition goes to the Assessor first, and a denial can be taken to the State Board of Equalization within 25 days or to court by December 15.

Who records the deed after a Gilbert sale?

The Maricopa County Recorder records it, usually through the title or escrow company handling the closing. Recording is $30 per instrument, including the $2 transfer fee, and the office can be reached at 602-506-3535 for general questions.

Permits for past work

Anything built under a permit needs a closed permit, and Chandler says missing ones tend to surface at sale time. You sign, the buyer's money arrives, and the deed gets recorded. With a cash buyer no underwriter reviews the file, so the calendar can shrink to a few weeks. Two snags show up late. A permit that was never finaled can stall a financed sale at the final hour, and an unpaid half of the tax bill comes out of your proceeds at the table. Clear both early.

Occupied or inherited houses need a possession date in writing. Ask the buyer whether belongings may stay or the rooms must be empty.

Start one folder with the parcel number, newest tax bill, HOA contact, repair notes and permit records. A buyer who reads it can price your house without a round of emails. Say early if the house is empty, inherited or rented out, since closing runs differently for each.

The standard fee is $30 per document. The deed must also carry an affidavit of property value or an exemption code.

Yes. Each rental location needs a city short-term rental license, plus a state Transaction Privilege Tax license and county rental registration. Operating without one can draw a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per month.

Scottsdale is long and narrow, about 31 miles from north to south, with Phoenix on the west and the McDowell Mountains on the east. Population is 243,006, and households are small at 2.03 people on average. Residents 65 and older make up 26.4 percent of the city. Owners occupy 67.0 percent of homes, which leaves about a third of households renting. Median gross rent is $2,013 and median household income is $110,886, which is why some buyers will want to know what your house could earn as a rental.

Buyers think of the city in four areas:

  • South Scottsdale, from McKellips Road north to Thomas Road, which includes the SkySong research center tied to Arizona State University
  • Old Town, the downtown core of galleries, restaurants and older streets
  • Central Scottsdale, also called the Shea Corridor, from Camelback Road north to Shea Boulevard
  • North Scottsdale, the northern end of the city

Name your area when you request offers. Comparable sales a mile apart can differ a great deal in price.

Several school districts divide the city. Scottsdale Unified covers most of the city, Paradise Valley Unified covers North Scottsdale, and Cave Creek Unified, Fountain Hills Unified, Balsz Elementary and Phoenix Union High School districts cover the remaining pieces. Confirm the district for your exact address before an ad mentions a school.

Short-term rental rules a buyer may ask about

Any Scottsdale rental shorter than 30 days needs a city license; longer leases are exempt. The annual license costs $250 per property. A buyer planning nightly or weekly stays should know the steps before bidding, and you can use them as a selling point if the house has been run this way.

An operator follows these steps:

  • Obtain a Transaction Privilege Tax license for each rental from the Arizona Department of Revenue, entering Scottsdale (SC) as the region code
  • Apply for the Scottsdale license under Ordinance 4566
  • Within 30 days of getting the license, tell the neighbors next door and across the street, and hold liability coverage of at least $500,000
  • Register the property with the Maricopa County Assessor before anyone occupies it
  • Post the required notice inside the front door and the backyard door

A property with a pool, hot tub or spa also faces pool barrier rules. Arizona law (A.R.S. 9-500.39) restricts what a city may demand here; a permit fee cannot exceed the actual cost or $250, whichever is lower. Call the City of Scottsdale licensing office to learn whether a license already exists for your address and what happens to it at sale.

Recording the deed in Maricopa County

Your sale is made public record when the deed reaches the Maricopa County Recorder. Each deed travels with an affidavit of property value, unless it names an exemption (A.R.S. 11-1133). That form reports the price, how the buyer is financing, the parcel number, the sale date and whether someone will live in the home or rent it. Gifts and nominal-consideration transfers among parent and child, spouses or siblings are exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134, along with a few other cases.

Most documents cost $30 to record, copies run $1 per page and a certification costs $3. Escrow or title staff usually submit the deed for you, and the closing statement lists the final charge, so a trip to the office is rarely needed.

At a typical closing the sequence runs like this: the title company confirms who owns the house and what liens attach, you and the buyer sign, funds are released, and the deed is sent for recording. Bring a photo ID and any paperwork about liens, a mortgage payoff or a tenant to the title office so nothing delays the signing.

Property tax due dates and what to do before you list

Tax bills split into two payments. The county treats a payment as late once 5:00 p.m. passes on the dates below (A.R.S. 42-18052).

InstallmentDue dateDelinquent after 5:00 p.m.
First halfOctober 1November 1
Second halfMarch 1May 1

Unpaid 2025 taxes get a final delinquent notice on December 1. Anyone paying a 2026 full-year bill above $100 in one lump has until December 31 to avoid interest.

Before listing, request the present balance for your parcel from the Maricopa County Treasurer. Closing then splits the current year between you and the buyer, and any amount still owed usually comes out of your sale proceeds, so learn the figure early.

If you cannot pay before listing, tell your buyer or agent at the start. A cash buyer can account for the balance in the offer, and the title company will show it as a line item at closing, so an unpaid bill rarely blocks a sale. It does help to ask for the payoff figure in writing so every party works from the same number.

Often faster than a financed sale, since no lender has to appraise the house or approve a loan. Title work, liens, probate and signing schedules still set the real date, so get the buyer to commit to one in writing.

Do I need a Scottsdale license to sell a house that was a short-term rental?

The license covers operating a rental of under 30 days, so ask the City of Scottsdale licensing office what happens to yours when the property sells. A new owner who keeps renting short term should expect to apply for their own.

What does it cost to record a deed in Maricopa County?

Most documents cost $30, with copies at $1 per page and a certification at $3. The $30 figure also appears in state statute A.R.S. 11-475.

Which school district is my Scottsdale home in?

Your street decides it. Most of the city sits in Scottsdale Unified and North Scottsdale in Paradise Valley Unified, while smaller areas fall under Cave Creek, Fountain Hills, Balsz or Phoenix Union. Verify with the district before advertising any school.

When are Scottsdale property taxes due?

Payments are due October 1 and March 1 and turn delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. A 2026 full-year payment avoids interest through December 31. The County Treasurer can give you your parcel balance.

In the desert heat, the cooling system is the item buyers care about most. An incomplete affidavit means the recorder must turn the deed away. Note that the sale date on the form is the day the contract was signed, rather than the closing date.

Your title company prepares and files this package, but read the affidavit before you sign it. A typical closing runs in order: the title company searches the record and requests payoffs, you and the buyer sign, funds are released, and the deed is recorded.

The tradeoff is price. A cash offer is usually lower than a well-prepared listing, and the buyer expects to handle repairs. Treat the offer as one number among several and ask each buyer to list what they charge and what they cover.

Before you contact buyers

A few items make offers faster and more accurate:

  • Your mortgage payoff balance, if you have a loan
  • A short list of repairs and any open permits you already know about
  • The lease and rent amount, if tenants live in the house
  • The community's resale rules, if the house is in an age-restricted neighborhood
  • The deadline by which you need the sale proceeds

With those in hand, a buyer can tell you a closing date, who pays recording and title charges, and whether repairs are priced in. If any of those answers is vague, ask again until it is written down.

City permits and rentals

Planning, permits and building safety all sit in the city's Community Development Department. If you have an open permit, or finished work without one, ask Community Development how to handle it before you list. An inspector or a lender may spot work that was done without a permit, and buyers react better when you disclose it first.

The city also runs a Rental Accountability Ordinance under Code Enforcement. If the house is rented now, ask Surprise Code Enforcement what that ordinance requires of you and what a buyer takes on.

A separate state rule, A.R.S. 9-500.39, restricts what cities may require of short-term rentals. A permit fee cannot exceed $250 or the cost of issuing it, and the city may ask for an emergency contact and proof of $500,000 in liability insurance.

Recording the deed in Maricopa County

Once you close, the Maricopa County Recorder receives the signed deed. It travels with an affidavit of property value signed by both sides or their agents (A.R.S. 11-1133), and a deed without that form is rejected unless it states an exemption. Gifts, nominal-consideration transfers inside a family and conveyances ordered by a court are exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134.

Recording runs $30 for most documents, with $1 per page on copies and $3 to certify one. Your escrow officer typically does the filing, and the closing statement itemizes what was charged.

The order is simple. A title company searches the record, both sides sign, money changes hands, and then the deed is recorded. Show up with a photo ID plus any papers about a loan payoff or tenants so nothing stalls the signing.

Property tax due dates

Two payments make up the yearly bill under A.R.S. 42-18052. If a deadline lands on a weekend, it slides to the next business day.

Unpaid 2025 taxes receive final delinquent notices on December 1. Paying a 2026 full-year bill above $100 in one sum avoids interest through December 31, and a bill of $100 or less turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. that day.

Phone the Maricopa County Treasurer for your parcel balance ahead of any signature. At closing the title company divides the current year between you and the buyer and deducts any unpaid amount from your proceeds.

An open tax balance will not block a sale. If the balance is still open when you accept an offer, tell the buyer early. A cash buyer can fold the amount into the price, and a title company treats it like any other payoff on the settlement sheet. Ask for the figure in writing so everyone is looking at the same number on closing day.

Speed depends on condition, price and how you sell. The city has grown 22.5 percent since the April 2020 estimates base, so many nearby sales are available for comparison. Weigh what each route would leave you in your pocket.

Which county records a Surprise home sale?

Maricopa County. The deed is filed with the Maricopa County Recorder for $30 in most cases. An affidavit of property value or a stated exemption must go with it.

Do I need a permit to sell a house with unpermitted work in Surprise?

Start with Surprise Community Development, which can explain how the city treats work done without a permit. Tell the buyer what you know, since an inspection or loan review may uncover it anyway.

Which school district serves my Surprise address?

Dysart Unified serves most of the city and Nadaburg Unified serves a small northern section. Call the district to verify your address before listing.

Can I sell a rented house in Surprise with tenants in it?

Check your lease and your notice duties first, and ask Surprise Code Enforcement about the Rental Accountability Ordinance. If a buyer wants the tenants to remain, get that in writing before accepting.

Goodyear is one of the fastest-growing places in the Phoenix area, about 17 miles west of downtown. Code Compliance responds to complaints about anything visible from the public right of way, so walk the front and sides of the house the way a neighbor or inspector would. Minor jobs, such as a residential pool or spa built from approved standard plans, go through the EZ Permit lane and are reviewed within five business days. An owner who rents out a Goodyear house must register it with the Maricopa County Assessor under A.R.S. 33-1902. Article 11-1-21, the Residential Rental Property Ordinance, sets minimum health and safety standards for the interior and exterior of any apartment, single-family home or mobile home rented for a fee.

Short stays have their own program. With a cash buyer, the lender is gone. Nobody needs an appraisal, nobody orders repairs as a loan condition, and you skip the weeks of showings a listing needs. Escrow and title still run the closing, so your liens, tax split and deed work the same way as in any sale.

Goodyear limits households to four pets, and it lets a property store no more than two recreational vehicles, trailers or boats in the side or rear yard, on a paved surface behind a solid six foot fence.

Do I need a permit for a fence in Goodyear?

Generally not for fences under six feet, but exceptions can apply. Front yard fences may reach three feet and rear yard fences six feet. Call the Development Counter at 623-932-3004 before building.

Half is due October 1 and half is due March 1. The first half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the second after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, with a weekend November 1 moving to the next business day.

Selling a house in an HOA

Under A.R.S. 33-1806, an association with 50 or more properties works from your notice. Tell it in writing that you accepted an offer and pass along the buyer's contact information. Construction applications go to the city's Permit Center at 39700 W Civic Center Plaza, and plans are submitted digitally through the online portal. Counter hours run Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., with Fridays closed. To get the permit history for your address, call (520) 316-6920 or write to dsd@maricopa-az.gov.

New codes came in this year. An expired or unfinished permit is worth resolving before escrow. Ask the Permit Center what closing it out would involve today. Lenders and inspectors notice open permits, and they are cheaper to fix while you still control the timeline.

The population was 57,144 in 2020 and is estimated at 59,358 on July 1, 2025. Households average 2.04 people, 73.2 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and residents 65 and over are 35.2 percent of the total. Collect these documents before you list:

Desert heat and your records

Few Arizona towns are hotter, so a buyer checks the cooling system first. Summer days routinely reach 110 degrees, temperatures can pass 100 as early as April and as late as October, and July and August nights often stay between 80 and 90 degrees. Rainfall averages only about 4.16 inches a year, and winter highs run in the 60s and 70s. Dry air and strong sun punish roofing, exterior paint, window seals and pool equipment.

Because lots here have been sold since the 1960s, some houses are decades old. A folder of records answers a buyer's questions about wiring, plumbing and roofs:

  • Electric and water bills for the hottest months, since buyers ask about summer costs

These records help a buyer judge risk, and they back up your asking price if an offer arrives lower than you hoped.

The city's Building Permits page lists the jobs that need a permit: room additions, patio covers, detached structures over 200 square feet, swimming pools and spas, gas lines, electrical panel change-outs, rewires, photovoltaic systems, fireplace installations, wall removal and added or relocated plumbing fixtures. Retaining walls over 2 feet 6 inches on a slope, or 3 feet on level ground, also need one.

Smaller jobs do not. Painting, floor covering, minor drywall repair, replacing roof covering, replacing an existing water heater and replacing an existing air conditioner without increasing its weight, capacity, location or ampacity all go without a permit. Code Enforcement pays attention to unscreened unlicensed vehicles, trash or debris visible from the street, structures in setback areas, and living in an RV or travel trailer for more than 7 days per calendar quarter on an improved residential lot. A buyer can run a vacation rental here, but needs a local business license. The development code lists a vacation rental dwelling in its permitted uses table and requires the operator to hold a valid local business license.

State law caps what the city may do. Under A.R.S. 9-500.39 a city or town may not prohibit short-term rentals, may charge a permit fee of no more than the actual cost or $250, whichever is less, and may require owners to give neighbors notice, provide emergency contact information and carry at least $500,000 of liability insurance. A first verified violation can bring a penalty of up to $500 or one night's advertised rent, whichever is greater.

If you rented the house by the night, give buyers the license number, tax registration and insurance details. If you did not, say that plainly. For the current permit fee or ordinance requirement, call the city's licensing office, since fees change.

Property tax and recording

The Mohave County Treasurer bills property tax in two installments. The first half is due October 1 and becomes past due after 5:00 p.m. on November 1, or the next business day when November 1 is a weekend. The second half is due March 1 and past due after May 1, which falls on a Saturday in 2027, so it moves to May 3, 2027. Bills over $100 paid in full by December 31 owe no interest accrued after November 1, and late payments accrue 16 percent annually, prorated monthly.

The Treasurer has a payment drop box at the county building, 2001 College Drive, Suite 93. Use a sealed envelope with the payment stub and a check or money order payable to the Mohave County Treasurer, and no cash. Confirm with your escrow officer how the tax year will be split at closing.

Lake Havasu City has its own Mohave County Recorder office at the same address, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. with a lunch closure from 12 to 1, phone (928) 453-0702 ext. 3021. Lake Havasu Unified School District No. 1 serves the city, with six elementary schools, one middle school and one high school. Names include Jamaica, Starline, Smoketree, Nautilus and Havasupai elementary schools, Oro Grande Classical Academy, Thunderbolt Middle School and Lake Havasu High School. Buyers with children will ask which school a home feeds, so look up the attendance information with the district before you list.

Closing on a Lake Havasu City house

After you accept an offer, escrow opens with a title company. The officer searches for liens, gets your payoff statements, divides the year's property tax and prepares the deed and affidavit for recording. A cash purchase has no lender review, so the pace depends on title work and permits. If a buyer's inspector finds an unpermitted pool or addition, expect a request to close the permit, lower the price or accept the house as is. Yes, but expect questions. Buyers' inspectors and lenders may ask for permit history on pools, additions and patio covers. How hot is Lake Havasu City, and does it matter when I sell?

Very hot. Summer days regularly reach 110 degrees, and the state's record of 128 degrees Fahrenheit was set here. Buyers focus on the air conditioner, roof and pool equipment, so service records help your price hold up.

Does Lake Havasu City allow vacation rentals?

Yes. The development code lists a vacation rental dwelling in its permitted uses table and requires the operator to have a valid local business license. State law also bars a city from prohibiting short-term rentals, though it may require a permit and neighbor notice.

Where do I record a deed in Lake Havasu City?

At the Mohave County Recorder office at 2001 College Drive, Suite 93, or at the main office in Kingman. The county lists a $30 fee, and the deed needs an Affidavit of Property Value or an exemption number. Your title company usually handles this for you at closing.

When is the next Mohave County property tax payment due?

The second half of 2026 taxes is due March 1, 2027 and becomes past due after 5 p.m. on May 3, 2027, because May 1 falls on a Saturday. Paying both halves in one payment by December 31, 2026 removes interest that accrued after November 1.

Housing figures show who buys here. Median value of an owner-occupied home is $321,900, owners occupy 69.7% of homes, and owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,533 a month. Median gross rent is $1,806 and median household income is $78,050. With 3.24 people per household, families looking for extra bedrooms and a yard are frequent buyers. The mean trip to work takes 30.1 minutes, so many people commute across the Valley.

Because the city is small, buyers often find a house by its cross streets and the school it feeds. Use both when you describe yours, and give the nearest major road so commuters see the drive at a glance.

Selling fast: your realistic options

An El Mirage owner has three roads. An agent listing exposes the house to the most buyers, but it hangs on showings, the buyer's loan and an appraisal. A sale by owner keeps the commission in your pocket and puts contracts and disclosure forms on your desk. A cash buyer takes the house exactly as it is and may close quickly, with an offer that prices in the repairs and risk.

Let the house and the calendar choose. A tidy, updated home and plenty of time points to a listing. Old repairs, a tenant, an inherited title or a hard deadline point to a direct sale. Whatever you pick, get offers in writing and compare the money you would actually keep.

Luke Air Force Base and aircraft noise

Luke Air Force Base, described as the largest fighter pilot training base in NATO, is close to El Mirage. Jets overhead are a normal subject for houses nearby, so expect a buyer to ask about the noise.

Arizona gives governments a way to put this on record. A.R.S. 28-8485 lets the state, or a political subdivision that operates an airport, designate an airport influence area, defined as property exposed to aircraft noise and overflight. The designating body files a record with the county recorder, which warns owners and would-be purchasers. Find out from your title company or the Maricopa County Recorder whether your parcel lies in a recorded area. Then tell the buyer the answer before the question comes up.

Permits and rental registration

El Mirage requires a permit for new construction, some repairs and alterations, and the remodeling, renovation or enlargement of a building. Building safety and permitting sit in the Development Services department. Since January 2, 2024 the Permit Center has taken all plans online through the ELM Online Permitting portal, and the same department schedules building inspections.

If an earlier owner finished a garage, patio or room addition, request its permit and inspection record from Development Services before you take an offer. Buyers who dream of an addition may also read the General Plan and the zoning ordinance update that Planning and Zoning maintains.

If the house has been rented, the Maricopa County Assessor shows the parcel type as Residential/Rental once a registration is on file. Ask Development Services whether a rental license or short-term rental registration applies to your address.

Schools for the listing description

The Dysart Unified School District serves El Mirage and enrolls roughly 5,500 preK through 12th grade students who live in the city. Elementary schools include El Mirage Elementary, Surprise Elementary, Thompson Ranch Elementary and Riverview Elementary. Dysart Middle School opened in 2021, and the high school choices are Dysart High School, opened in 1963, and Sundown Mountain, an alternative school for 11th and 12th grades. Some residents north of Waddell and Thunderbird Roads are zoned for Valley Vista High School, which sits outside the city.

The zone for your street may differ from a neighbor's. Use the district's boundary lookup for your exact address before you write the listing.

Maricopa County bills El Mirage owners twice a year.

InstallmentDueDelinquent after
First halfOctober 1November 1, after 5 p.m.
Second halfMarch 1May 1, after 5 p.m.

When the first of November lands on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day. A bill over $100 can be paid in full through December 31 without interest. Phone the county treasurer for your parcel's balance before closing, so nothing unpaid turns up at the title company.

Deed, affidavit and recording

A sale of an El Mirage house goes on record at the Maricopa County Recorder, for $30 on most documents. Staff there will not take a deed unless it shows an affidavit of property value or an exemption code, and they will not tell you which code is yours. Walk the paperwork into 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200, Phoenix, or mail it and wait two to four weeks for the originals to return.

The affidavit comes from A.R.S. 11-1133 and asks for the price, sale date, legal description and parcel details. Exemptions live in A.R.S. 11-1134. They cover a deed of gift, a quitclaim given for no money, a conveyance ordered by a court, and a nominal-consideration transfer between spouses, siblings, parents and children, or grandparents and grandchildren. When a family settles a house after a death, one of these often applies. A title officer or attorney can say which.

What a cash sale skips

A cash purchase drops three hurdles that slow a financed deal: the buyer's loan approval, the lender's appraisal, and the repair list a loan can require. Escrow and title still happen, so liens, taxes and the deed move through the same hands. The difference is how long it takes and how many outside parties can stall it.

Before you talk to any buyer, collect your parcel number, newest tax bill, any mortgage payoff figure, and permit records for the garage, patio or additions. Mention aircraft noise, an open permit or a tenant at the outset. A problem found late usually costs you more than one disclosed early.

After you accept, plan your move-out date with the buyer and confirm in writing whether furniture or leftover items may stay. Keep copies of everything you sign, and save the closing statement for your tax records.

Frequently asked questions

How many people live in El Mirage?

The population is 35,820 as of July 1, 2025, nearly the same as the 35,805 counted in 2020. The city covers 9.95 square miles.

Which school district serves El Mirage?

The Dysart Unified School District serves the city, and its schools include El Mirage Elementary, Thompson Ranch Elementary, Riverview Elementary and Dysart High School. Some residents north of Waddell and Thunderbird Roads are zoned for Valley Vista High School.

What does it cost to record a deed in Maricopa County?

The Maricopa County Recorder charges $30 per document for deeds and most other filings. A deed also needs an affidavit of property value or an exemption code before it is accepted.

Is El Mirage close to Luke Air Force Base?

Yes, and aircraft noise is a normal question from buyers. Ask your title company whether an airport influence area is recorded against your parcel.

Do I need a permit to repair a house in El Mirage?

A permit is needed for new construction, some repair work, alterations, remodeling, renovation or enlargement. Plans go in online through the city's permit portal, and Development Services can tell you whether a specific job is covered.

Selling a house in Florence, AZ

Florence, the Pinal County seat, lies on the Gila River's south bank at about 1,539 feet, with State Routes 79 and 287 running through. The population is 25,222 as of July 1, 2025. Owners occupy 86.8% of homes, the median owner-occupied value is $346,300, and median gross rent is $1,302. The town counts 6,719 households of 2.39 people each, and the mean commute is 30.9 minutes. Newer subdivisions, such as an Anthem community roughly six miles northwest of the old townsite, share the map with the historic core, so a street two miles away may price very differently. Look at recent sales close to yours, because an average for the whole town tells you little about one street.

Owners in a hurry can accept a cash offer for the house in its present state, or list it and wait for a buyer who needs financing. Condition, timing and occupancy usually settle it:

  • Cash, as-is: inherited property, postponed repairs, tenants in place, or a seller who has to move.
  • Agent listing: a house ready to move into, with an owner who can stand showings and an inspection period.
  • Sale by owner: a seller who already knows the buyer and is comfortable with the contract and title steps.

Florence Historic District

A house inside the Florence Historic District may carry preservation compliance steps, so find out early whether your address falls within it. The Town's historic preservation staff works with the Historic District Advisory Commission, homeowners, developers and the State Historic Preservation Office on preservation laws, compliance procedures, rehabilitation standards and financial incentives. The district includes more than 25 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places.

Before listing an older house, ask the Town's Community Development Department two questions. Is the property in the district? Would a planned repair, such as new windows or a new porch, trigger a compliance step? A buyer who plans to fix up the house will ask the same things, and a clear answer from you saves a week of back and forth.

Older houses near the downtown streets often come with decades of small changes: an enclosed porch, a swapped window, a rebuilt wall. Write down what was changed and when, and keep any receipts. That list will answer most of an inspector's questions before they are asked, and it shows a cash buyer exactly what they are taking on.

Property tax payments

Florence owners get a Pinal County bill with two payments.

InstallmentDueDelinquent after
First halfOctober 15 p.m. on November 1
Second halfMarch 15 p.m. on May 1

A bill of $100 or less is due in full on October 1. When November 1 lands on a weekend, the cutoff slides to the next business day.

  • Interest runs at 16% a year, prorated monthly, and the Treasurer has no power to waive it.
  • Settling the whole year by December 31 wipes out interest on the first half.
  • A parcel with unpaid taxes can land in the online tax lien sale held each February.
  • September bills are a courtesy mailing, not a requirement. Keep your address current with the Assessor at 520-866-6361 so you do not miss one.

Give the escrow officer your payment status the day escrow opens, so the closing statement divides the year properly. Ask the Treasurer's office in Florence about any balance you are unsure of.

How to appeal your valuation

If the Notice of Value looks too high, move fast. You have 60 days from the mailing date to petition the Pinal County Assessor, and filing costs nothing. Residential owners use Form 82130R, and a meeting with the appraisers is optional. Rulings are due by August 15.

Know what the appeal can and cannot do. Only the full cash value can be challenged, while the tax itself is figured on the limited property value, which in most cases rises no faster than 5% a year. When the limited value already sits under the figure you consider fair, a win leaves your bill unchanged.

A denial goes next to the Pinal County Board of Equalization, within 25 days. Court is the last step, within 60 days of the final decision. Stay current on payments throughout, because a parcel in court that goes delinquent gets the case dismissed. Bring recent sales of similar Florence houses to any meeting, and tell the buyer if an appeal is still open at closing.

Recording the deed in Pinal County

Deeds for Florence sales are recorded at the Pinal County Recorder, 31 N Pinal Street, Building E, Florence (520-866-6830). In person, by mail and through approved electronic partners all work, though most sales arrive by way of the title company.

  • Both sides complete the affidavit of property value. Leaving it out is a class 2 misdemeanor. A transfer that qualifies for an exemption carries a notation such as A.R.S. 11-1134 B3 in its place.
  • Walking a document in? Bring valid government photo identification, required since September 14, 2026. Escrow and title companies, banks, active State Bar members and government agencies are exempt.
  • Recorded copies run $1 per page, plus $3 for certification.
  • Sign up for the Assessor's Parcel Alert List to get a free notice whenever a deed is received on your parcel. It helps catch deed fraud.

The recording fee is set by statute at $30 per instrument, including a $2 transfer fee. Staff will not draft documents or advise you on legal questions.

Landlords and short-term hosts

Landlords should check that the house is on file with the Pinal County Assessor, because every Arizona county requires residential rental registration. Under A.R.S. 33-1902 an unregistered rental cannot be occupied, and changes must be reported within ten days.

Short-term rentals of 29 days or less fall under the state's transient lodging classification and the Town's hotel classification for transaction privilege tax. The Arizona Department of Revenue administers Florence's tax program, and its taxpayer line is 800-352-4090. Clear any back filings before closing, since underreported tax can bring interest and penalties.

What happens between offer and closing

Accepting an offer sends the file to a title company, where escrow begins. The officer hunts for liens, orders your mortgage payoff, apportions the year's tax and drafts the deed and affidavit. Without a lender, a cash purchase has no appraisal or underwriting, and timing comes down to title work and your move-out date. A loan adds both of those steps.

Pull together your parcel number, newest tax bill, repair and permit records, and any lease if tenants live there. For an inherited house, tell the title officer at once so the right documents get collected. Sellers who finish this homework before an offer lands rarely face last-minute delays.

On closing day, expect to sign the deed at the title office, hand over keys and garage openers, and leave the utilities set up so they can transfer to the new owner. Take dated photos of the empty house the day you leave, in case a question comes up later.

Frequently asked questions

Which county records a deed after a Florence sale?

Pinal County. The Recorder's Office at 31 N Pinal Street, Building E in Florence records the deed, and it can be reached at 520-866-6830. Most sales are submitted by the title or escrow company.

Do I need photo ID to record a document in Florence?

Yes, if you present it in person at the Pinal County Recorder. A valid government photo ID is required unless you are an escrow or title company, a bank or credit union, an active State Bar member or a government agency.

When do Pinal County taxes go delinquent?

The first half goes delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after 5 p.m. on May 1. Late payments accrue 16% interest a year, prorated monthly, and interest cannot be waived.

How long do I have to appeal my Florence home's value?

You have 60 days from the mailing date of the Notice of Value to file a petition with the Pinal County Assessor. There is no filing fee, and the Assessor must rule by August 15.

Does Florence have a historic district?

Yes. It has a National Historic District with more than 25 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places. The Town's preservation staff and Historic District Advisory Commission work with homeowners on compliance procedures and rehabilitation standards.
